cases.case_name: Weaver v. Roanoke Department of Human Resources
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the termination of both parents' residual parental rights because the record contained no evidence that social agencies made the 'reasonable and appropriate efforts' that Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) requires before rights may be severed, and directed that termination statutes be read to preserve the parent-child relationship where possible.
cases.quote: Statutes terminating the legal relationship between parent and child should be interpreted consistently with the governmental objective of preserving, when possible, the parent-child relationship.

relevance.INP-05: Virginia's foundational termination case arises from children placed in foster care partly at the parents' own request, and holds that the agency, not the family, bears the burden of showing services were offered.
relevance.DEC-06: Because termination cannot rest on conditions the agency never tried to remedy, the decision supplies the legal reason a Virginia agency may respond with services rather than a petition.
relevance.ACT-01: The Court reversed termination where the record showed no agency assistance was ever offered, which is the direct legal consequence of skipping voluntary services.
relevance.ACT-02: It fixes the constraint on court-ordered service plans: the plan and the efforts behind it must appear in the record or termination cannot follow.
relevance.OUT-01: The opinion states Virginia's governing preference for preserving the parent-child relationship, the legal anchor for reunification as the default outcome.

cases.case_name: Knox v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination and held that under Code § 16.1-283 a court need make no separate finding of parental unfitness, because a finding of the statutory factors plus the child's best interests is itself equivalent to a finding of unfitness.
cases.quote: In our opinion, a finding that the factors exist is tantamount to a finding of parental unfitness.

relevance.ACT-02: It confirms that a parent's failure over years to comply with agency rehabilitative services is itself the statutory predicate, so the content of the court-ordered service record controls the case.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the controlling Virginia statement of what a court must find to terminate: best interests plus the enumerated § 16.1-283 factors, with no additional unfitness finding required.

cases.case_name: Toombs v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that whether parental visitation must continue after a termination petition is filed is decided case by case with the child's best interests as the guiding principle, and that clear and convincing evidence supported the statutory factors here.
cases.quote: The question must be resolved, however, in light of the facts of each case, with the best interests of the child as the guiding principle.

relevance.INP-05: The children entered foster care through the parents' own approach to the agency, and the Court still required the Division to prove the statutory grounds by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.DEC-05: Once the Division filed its termination petitions the legal posture changed, and the Court measured the agency's suspension of visitation against the best-interests standard.
relevance.ACT-01: It treats the services the Division actually offered the parents as the measure of whether the family's failure to correct conditions was 'without good cause'.
relevance.ACT-03: The decision governs contact between parent and child during the foster-care period once a termination petition is pending.
relevance.OUT-01: Suspension of visitation is scrutinized here precisely because continued contact is the practical path back to reunification.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the companion case applying the § 16.1-283(C)(2) clear-and-convincing standard to affirm termination.

cases.case_name: Harris v. Lynchburg Division of Social Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination as to the mother but reversed as to the father, holding that undisputed evidence that a parent was never offered or provided services overcomes the statutory prima facie case and puts the agency to full proof of the § 16.1-283(C)(2) factors.
cases.quote: where, as here, there is undisputed evidence that a parent has not been offered or provided services, the prima facie case is overcome

relevance.INP-05: A parent who never asked for and was never offered help cannot be terminated on a prima facie showing alone.
relevance.DEC-06: It is the strongest Virginia authority that the agency must actually engage a parent with services before the case can escalate to a termination petition.
relevance.ACT-01: This is the controlling Virginia rule that the failure to offer voluntary services defeats termination even when the statutory prima facie triggers are met.
relevance.OUT-01: The Court ordered the father given the offer and an opportunity to show what progress he could make, i.e., a genuine chance at reunification.

cases.case_name: Richardson v. Henry County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B)(2), holding that proof that the mother without good cause failed to respond to available and reasonable rehabilitative efforts is statutory prima facie evidence of the (B)(2) conditions, which the mother then failed to rebut.
cases.quote: Under the statute, this is prima facie evidence of the conditions set forth in subparagraph (B)(2) of the statute.

relevance.DEC-06: It identifies the documented menu of voluntary services (counseling, employment referral, housing, mental health) that the agency must show before escalation is justified.
relevance.ACT-01: The extensive list of services the Department made available is what converted the case into a prima facie termination case when the mother did not respond.
relevance.ACT-02: It is the Virginia authority on how a parent's non-response to a court-supervised service regime shifts the burden of going forward.

cases.case_name: Walker v. Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed and remanded because the circuit court wrongly placed the burden on the parents: an appeal from the juvenile court is tried de novo, only final orders are appealable, and on a § 16.1-283 termination petition the Department must carry the clear-and-convincing burden in the circuit court.
cases.quote: such a trial de novo in the circuit court grants to a litigant every advantage which would have been his had the case been tried originally in such court

relevance.INP-04: It maps the statutory route by which a juvenile and domestic relations court order moves into circuit court, which is the procedural spine of every court-initiated child welfare case in Virginia.
relevance.DEC-05: It distinguishes a custody petition from a petition to terminate residual parental rights and fixes who bears the burden on each.
relevance.FAIL-01: This is the leading Virginia case reversing a lower court for misallocating the burden of proof on appeal from the juvenile court, and for treating a non-final interlocutory order as binding.

cases.case_name: Doe v. Doe
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed a decree of adoption that had severed a mother's parental rights on the basis of her lesbian relationship, holding that sexual orientation does not make a parent unfit per se and that adoption over a parent's objection requires proof that continuing the relationship would be detrimental to the child.
cases.quote: We decline to hold that every lesbian mother or homosexual father is per se an unfit parent.

relevance.ACT-04: The petitioners were the child's paternal relatives, and the Court held the relatives' preferred placement could not displace the natural parent absent proof of detriment.
relevance.FAIL-05: This is the Virginia Supreme Court's controlling rejection of status-based disqualification of a parent, the state analogue to a discrimination claim in placement decisions.

cases.case_name: Lynchburg Division of Social Services v. Cook
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed the Court of Appeals and held that once the foster care statutory process has begun, a court may not transfer custody of the child to a relative other than the prior family without making, and stating in the order, the four specific findings required by Code §§ 16.1-278.2(A1), 16.1-281(C1), 16.1-282(D1) and 16.1-282.1(A1).
cases.quote: Those findings, under the plain terms of the statutes, must be stated in the order transferring custody.

relevance.INP-04: The opinion sets out the full sequence of judicially ordered steps — emergency removal, preliminary removal, dispositional, foster care plan, review, and permanency hearings — that court involvement triggers.
relevance.INP-12: It recites the § 16.1-251(A) emergency-removal showing: imminent threat of severe or irremediable injury, reasonable efforts to prevent removal, and no less drastic alternative.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the Supreme Court of Virginia's authoritative statement of what must be proved for an emergency or preliminary removal order.
relevance.DEC-05: It explains how a dependency case is opened and what findings each successive statutory hearing requires.
relevance.ACT-03: It holds that the specific foster care statutes, not the general custody statutes, control once a child is subject to a foster care plan.
relevance.ACT-04: This is the controlling Virginia authority that kinship transfers out of foster care require four express statutory findings stated in the order.
relevance.ACT-05: It catalogs the protective dispositional powers the juvenile court may exercise after an abuse or neglect finding under Code § 16.1-278.2.
relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship or kinship permanency achieved during a foster care case is invalid unless the order contains the four mandated findings.

cases.case_name: Copeland v. Todd
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reinstated the adoption decree, holding that Virginia's adoption statutes satisfy Fourteenth Amendment due process because the Code § 63.2-1205 factors require consideration of parental fitness and the effect on the child, so courts may not graft an additional judicially created 'detriment to the child' finding onto the statute.
cases.quote: Rather, for these statutes to pass constitutional due process scrutiny, they must provide for consideration of parental fitness and detriment to the child.

relevance.INP-04: The circuit court acted on a court-ordered social services investigation and report, which is how a contested adoption brings the agency into a private proceeding.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the governing Virginia statement of the constitutional floor for adoption over a birth parent's withheld consent.
relevance.OUT-03: It fixes the standard a long-term custodian must meet to convert a de facto kinship or custodial placement into permanent legal status.

cases.case_name: Bonanno v. Quinn
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed dismissal of a grandmother's appeal from an adoption order, holding that the phrase 'aggrieved party' in Code § 17.1-405 confers appellate standing only on those actually joined as litigants below, so a non-party who never moved to intervene cannot appeal.
cases.quote: confers standing to bring an appeal to the Court of Appeals only on those who were litigants joined in the proceeding from which the judgment appealed from was taken

relevance.INP-04: The case turns on a court-ordered social worker investigation in a sealed adoption proceeding and on what notice that investigation gave an interested relative.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the controlling Virginia rule on who may obtain appellate review of a child welfare or adoption order, and therefore on when an erroneous order becomes unreviewable.

cases.case_name: Mast v. A.A.
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed and dismissed a petition to vacate a final adoption order, holding that Code § 63.2-1216 is a legislative statute of repose that bars any collateral or direct attack on a final adoption order, for any reason including procedural failure or fraud, after six months.
cases.quote: Code § 63.2-1216 is a legislatively created statute of repose, not a judicially created procedural deadline.

relevance.INP-11: The case arose from a child found by the U.S. military abroad and adopted in Virginia, and is the Court's most recent treatment of competing federal, foreign and state claims over a child's placement.
relevance.OUT-03: It defines when a permanency order becomes absolutely unassailable, which is the outer boundary of any kinship or guardianship challenge.
relevance.OUT-02: It is the controlling Virginia authority on the finality of adoption decrees and the six-month repose on attacking them.

cases.case_name: Messina v. Burden
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia held that sovereign immunity extends to employees of immune local as well as state entities, applying the four-factor James test with the employing governmental entity substituted for the state, so that supervisory employees acting within the scope of employment are immune from claims of simple negligence.
cases.quote: Thus, in applying the James test to employees of other immune governmental entities, the word “state” should be deleted and the proper description of the governmental entity substituted.

relevance.FAIL-02: It is the controlling Virginia state-law immunity framework a family must overcome to sue a local department of social services worker in tort for an unlawful removal.
relevance.FAIL-04: A negligence claim arising from a child's death in agency care must clear this immunity test and plead more than simple negligence.
relevance.PMC-02: Immunity for discretionary local-government functions is what channels accountability for agency conduct into audit and oversight rather than damages litigation.

cases.case_name: Department of Corrections v. Surovell
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia held that VFOIA must be liberally construed toward disclosure and its exemptions narrowly construed, with the public body bearing the burden to establish an exemption by a preponderance of the evidence, though it found the security exemption satisfied on the record before it.
cases.quote: Disclosure exemptions must be “narrowly construed” in favor of disclosure.

relevance.INP-09: Systemic oversight of a Virginia agency begins with records access, and this case sets the presumption and burden that govern every VFOIA request to a public body.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the controlling Virginia rule that the agency, not the requester, bears the burden of justifying non-disclosure.
relevance.PMC-02: Audit and financial-oversight records held by a Virginia public body are presumptively disclosable under the standard stated here.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review of agency policy depends on the disclosure presumption and narrow-exemption rule announced in this case.
relevance.PMC-04: Fatality review data held by a Virginia public body is subject to this disclosure presumption unless the body carries its burden on an exemption.
relevance.PMC-05: This is the governing Virginia FOIA construction rule for any transparency demand made to a child welfare agency.
relevance.PMC-06: Any systematic public analysis of Virginia agency performance rests on the disclosure presumption and the agency's burden of proof described here.

cases.case_name: Edwards v. County of Arlington
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed and remanded a termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the county failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that the conditions producing the neglect could not be substantially corrected or eliminated so as to allow the child's safe return.
cases.quote: Upon this evidence we conclude that there was no clear and convincing showing made of the statutory criteria required to support an order terminating residual parental rights.

relevance.OUT-05: The Court's reversal restores the family's position where the agency's proof fell short of the statutory criteria, the appellate analogue of case dismissal.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a leading published Virginia example of appellate reversal for insufficient evidence supporting the agency's termination case, including scrutiny of the parent's language and cultural barriers.

cases.case_name: Jackson v. W.
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed, upholding the Department's child protective services guidelines and holding that a 'founded' disposition that only threatens reputation and speculative future consequences does not deprive the alleged abuser of a liberty or property interest requiring additional procedural safeguards.
cases.quote: However, a person’s reputation alone is not a liberty or property interest and thus is not entitled to due process protection.

relevance.INP-01: It describes the investigation and notification sequence that follows a report about a professional and holds the resulting departmental guidelines valid.
relevance.INP-02: A complaint from any source triggers the same three-stage investigate-conference-hearing process the Court validated here.
relevance.INP-06: The confidentiality provisions of the reporting and central registry statutes, which the Court relied on to find no cognizable stigma, are what make anonymous and confidential intake workable.
relevance.INP-08: For educators and other professionals a founded finding carries career consequences, and this case holds those consequences too speculative to require added process.
relevance.INP-09: The Court upheld the Commissioner's authority to adopt the child protective services guidelines against a vagueness and ultra vires challenge, which is the framework any oversight review must apply.
relevance.INP-10: It sets out the three-step escalation from initial investigative determination through local conference to the Commissioner's administrative hearing.
relevance.DEC-02: It holds the Department's function to be adjudicative as well as investigative, which is why the due process inquiry applies at all.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the leading Virginia case on what process is constitutionally due before and after a 'founded' disposition.
relevance.FAIL-06: The Court relied on the statutory confidentiality of investigation records and registry data to conclude no stigma could attach.
relevance.PMC-03: Review of the Department's own policy manual and guidelines against statutory authority is the model for external evaluation of CPS policy.
relevance.PMC-05: It identifies which CPS records are statutorily confidential and which are not, the starting point for any Virginia disclosure request.
relevance.PMC-06: The opinion supplies the balancing test — private interest, risk of error, government burden — for evaluating proposed procedural reforms to Virginia CPS.

cases.case_name: Turner v. Jackson
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed a founded disposition of physical abuse, holding that agency factfinding is reviewed only for substantial evidence and that a founded disposition, which does not itself alter custody or parental rights, works no deprivation of a protected liberty or property interest.
cases.quote: Review of agency factual decisions is governed by the “substantial evidence” test.

relevance.INP-10: It confirms that the escalation from investigation to a founded finding is reviewed on the agency record under the deferential substantial evidence test.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the companion case fixing both the standard of review of a founded disposition and the limits of the due process interest it implicates.

cases.case_name: J.P. v. Carter
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed a founded sexual abuse disposition, holding that neither the statute nor due process requires the investigator to contact the accused before entering the initial determination, because the statutory amendment request, local conference and Commissioner's hearing supply the process due.
cases.quote: While it is clearly preferable for an investigating official to contact the accused and any interested party, it is not a prerequisite to a valid determination.

relevance.INP-01: The investigation began with a report from the children's parents and shows what a reporter's allegation sets in motion against a named caretaker.
relevance.INP-08: The accused was working with children, and the case illustrates the registry consequences a school or childcare-connected finding carries.
relevance.INP-10: It traces the escalation from initial investigative determination through the statutory appeal ladder and holds that ladder constitutionally sufficient.
relevance.DEC-02: It is the controlling Virginia holding that pre-determination contact with the accused is preferred but not legally required to validate an investigation.
relevance.DEC-03: It states the due process framework and the eighteen-year central registry consequence attached to a founded, level one finding.

cases.case_name: Carter v. Gordon
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed the circuit court and reinstated the Department's findings that an elementary school physical education teacher sexually abused students, holding that the trial court improperly substituted its own factfinding for the agency's and that Gordon suffered no deprivation cognizable under the Due Process Clause.
cases.quote: Under the facts of this case, we hold the trial court improperly rejected the agency's findings and substituted its own.

relevance.INP-01: School employees who observed and relayed the students' accounts are the mandated reporters whose reports drove this investigation.
relevance.INP-08: This is the leading published Virginia case on a founded abuse disposition arising from disclosures in a school setting.
relevance.DEC-03: It fixes the deference a reviewing court owes the agency's founded disposition and the level assigned to each incident.

cases.case_name: C.S. v. Virginia Beach Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed, vacated and remanded a termination under Code § 16.1-283(C)(2), holding that the evidence fell short of clear and convincing proof that the mother had failed to remedy substantially the conditions leading to foster care placement.
cases.quote: the evidence falls short of the standard of clear and convincing proof that mother did not remedy substantially the conditions which led to the child's foster care placement

relevance.OUT-01: The Court found the mother had in fact remedied the conditions, restoring the reunification path the trial court had cut off.
relevance.OUT-05: Vacatur of the termination order on insufficient evidence is the appellate route to closing an unproven case.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is a published Virginia reversal of an agency-driven termination where the Court found nothing in the record supporting the trial court's conclusions, including an agency concern rooted in the mother's distrust of government.

cases.case_name: Jones v. West
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed dismissal of a founded sexual abuse complaint, holding that the local department's failure to tape record the child victim's interview, absent any specific determination that recording was impractical or inappropriate under 22 VAC 40-705-80(B)(1), violated required procedure and was not harmless error.
cases.quote: It was essential, therefore, for the hearing officer to have access to the precise substance of S.J.’s statements.

relevance.INP-03: The interview failure arose from the department's blanket deference to the police department's practice in a joint law enforcement investigation, which the Court held could not substitute for its own regulatory judgment.
relevance.INP-09: It shows that regulatory non-compliance discovered on review, not merely weak evidence, can invalidate an agency disposition.
relevance.INP-10: Escalation to a formal investigation carries binding procedural obligations that the agency cannot waive by policy.
relevance.DEC-02: This is the controlling Virginia authority on the mandatory interview and recording procedures a CPS investigation must follow.
relevance.DEC-03: A founded disposition must be set aside where a procedural violation could have had a significant impact on the ultimate decision.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court affirmed outright dismissal rather than remand, the strongest form of case closure for a wrongly investigated subject.
relevance.FAIL-01: It is the leading Virginia example of a court setting aside an agency finding for failure to observe required investigative procedure.

cases.case_name: Commissioner, Virginia Department of Social Services v. Fulton
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia reversed a circuit court that had converted a founded disposition to unfounded and purged the registry, holding that under the Administrative Process Act the reviewing court may reject agency factfinding only if a reasonable mind would necessarily reach a different conclusion, and may not reweigh witness credibility.
cases.quote: It is not the trial court’s role to determine the credibility of the witnesses.

relevance.DEC-01: It shows what a circuit court may and may not do when asked to convert a founded disposition to unfounded and purge the record.
relevance.DEC-03: This is the most recent published Virginia statement of the substantial-evidence standard governing review of a founded disposition and of the preponderance standard the agency itself applies.
relevance.OUT-05: It defines the narrow circumstances in which a court may order a complaint changed to unfounded and the records purged.
relevance.FAIL-01: It marks the limit of judicial reversal of agency findings: disagreement with the agency's credibility determinations is not enough.

cases.case_name: Dawn Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination of the mother's rights to all three children under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the statutory definitions of an abused or neglected child do not require proof of actual harm to each child and that abuse of a sibling plus an unsafe home environment supports the finding as to the others.
cases.quote: Thus, we hold that the evidence was sufficient to support the trial court’s determination that E. and W. were abused or neglected.

relevance.INP-07: The case originated in a hospital's findings of non-accidental trauma to an infant, the paradigm medical disclosure that opens a Virginia CPS case.
relevance.INP-12: It recites the Code § 16.1-251(A) emergency custody showing and holds that 'substantial risk' speaks prospectively, permitting removal before harm occurs.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the controlling Virginia authority that siblings of an injured child may be removed on risk alone without proof each was already harmed.
relevance.ACT-03: It supports foster care placement of non-injured siblings where the home environment still presents the requisite threat.
relevance.ACT-06: The infant's skull and rib fractures required emergency medical evaluation, and the medical findings became the evidentiary core of the abuse determination.
relevance.OUT-06: It addresses serious non-fatal injury to an infant under circumstances the trial court found non-accidental.

cases.case_name: Christopher Farrell v. Warren County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination and rejected the father's due process challenge, holding that Code § 16.1-283(B) is constitutional because the Department must prove every element supporting termination by clear and convincing evidence even though the underlying abuse or neglect adjudication uses a preponderance standard.
cases.quote: In the context of terminating a parent’s rights, the Due Process Clause requires that the Department prove each of the necessary allegations of parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.INP-07: The medical evidence of the infant's injuries drove the adjudication, and the father's challenge to the standard of proof applied to it was rejected.
relevance.DEC-05: It holds that a petition must specifically request termination so that proper notice is given before that relief may be entered.
relevance.OUT-02: This is Virginia's leading published rejection of a constitutional attack on the § 16.1-283(B) termination scheme, confirming clear and convincing proof of unfitness is required.

cases.case_name: Patricia Tackett v. Arlington County Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination of the mother's rights and denial of the grandmother's custody petition, holding that a relative lacks standing to assert the parent's rights and may appeal only the permanency-goal findings and the disposition of her own custody petition.
cases.quote: Grandmother only has standing to appeal the circuit court’s findings made in connection with the change in permanency goal and with regard to grandmother’s petition for custody.

relevance.ACT-02: The grandmother's failure to complete the psychological evaluation and employment verification required by the foster care plan is what defeated her custody petition.
relevance.ACT-04: This is the controlling Virginia case on a relative caregiver's limited standing when the agency removes a child from her guardianship and changes the goal to adoption.
relevance.OUT-03: It shows that a prior guardianship does not survive removal and does not give the relative standing to contest termination of the parent's rights.

cases.case_name: Adam Yafi v. Stafford Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(E), holding that where a parent is convicted of felony child abuse causing serious bodily injury to a sibling or subjects a child to aggravated circumstances, the Department need not prove it offered reasonable and appropriate rehabilitative services.
cases.quote: the termination of Yafi’s residual parental rights under Code § 16.1-283(E)(iii) and 16.1-283(E)(iv) did not require a predicate showing that DSS provided any services to Yafi

relevance.INP-07: The case arose from a half-sibling's hospitalization for serious bodily injury, the medical disclosure pathway into a Virginia abuse case.
relevance.ACT-06: The sibling's life-threatening injuries required emergency medical care, and the resulting felony conviction became the statutory ground for termination.
relevance.OUT-01: It identifies the aggravated-circumstances situations in which Virginia law removes reunification and reasonable efforts from the case entirely.
relevance.OUT-02: This is the leading published Virginia authority on the § 16.1-283(E) aggravated-circumstances route to termination, including for an incarcerated parent.
relevance.OUT-06: It defines 'serious bodily injury' under Code § 16.1-283(E) as injury involving substantial risk of death, extreme pain, disfigurement or protracted loss of function.

cases.case_name: Norfolk Department of Human Services v. Goldberg
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed an order releasing CPS investigation records, holding that the bad faith disclosure exception in Code § 63.2-1514(D) reaches reports conveyed to the Department by an innocent mandatory reporter when the underlying allegation originated with someone acting maliciously or in bad faith.
cases.quote: Consistent with the statute’s purpose, we find that Code § 63.2-1514(D) covers bad faith disclosures made to mandatory reporters.

relevance.INP-01: This is the controlling Virginia case on what happens when a mandatory reporter innocently relays an allegation that originated with a bad-faith accuser.
relevance.INP-02: It construes the statutory remedy available to the subject of an unfounded third-party report made maliciously.
relevance.INP-06: The suspected originator may have reported anonymously, and the Court held anonymity does not defeat the subject's right to the records.
relevance.DEC-01: It governs the records consequences of an unfounded disposition and the subject's route to obtain the investigative file.
relevance.ACT-05: The Department imposed a safety plan requiring the accused parent to leave the home during the investigation, the informal analogue of a protective order.
relevance.FAIL-05: It supplies the Virginia mechanism for a person targeted by a retaliatory or malicious report to obtain the records needed to seek civil relief.
relevance.FAIL-06: It is the leading published Virginia decision compelling a local department to disclose child protective services records over its objection.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the statutory boundary between CPS record confidentiality and an individual's right of access under Code § 63.2-1514(D).

cases.case_name: Jordan v. Jackson
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that Virginia's emergency removal scheme, which permits a child to be taken into protective custody before judicial review provided an ex parte or adversarial removal order is obtained as soon as possible and in no event later than seventy-two hours, is constitutional facially and as applied.
cases.quote: at least ex parte judicial review to ratify the initial removal decision must be obtained “as soon as possible,” but in any event within seventy-two hours

relevance.INP-03: Removal in this case followed a police and hospital referral, and the opinion describes the parallel law enforcement custody authority under Code § 16.1-246.
relevance.INP-12: This is the controlling federal authority upholding Virginia's protective custody statute and fixing the constitutional outer limit on unreviewed state custody.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the leading Fourth Circuit case on Virginia emergency removals, requiring that the delay before judicial ratification be measured by promptness.
relevance.ACT-05: It describes the ex parte and adversarial removal orders and the less-drastic-alternative findings Virginia courts must make.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the benchmark against which a Virginia wrongful removal claim under § 1983 is measured, since the plaintiffs' procedural challenge failed while their as-applied claim of no imminent danger proceeded.

cases.case_name: Wildauer v. Frederick County
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for the county, holding that a social worker's consented-to investigative home visit accompanied by deputies did not violate the Fourth Amendment because such visits are not measured by criminal search standards and consent to the caseworker's entry extended to the accompanying officials.
cases.quote: Furthermore, investigative home visits by social workers are not subject to the same scrutiny as searches in the criminal context.

relevance.INP-03: The caseworker was accompanied by sheriff's deputies, and the Court held their presence did not convert the consented entry into an unreasonable search.
relevance.INP-12: It defines the Fourth Amendment limits on a caseworker entering a home to take custody of children.
relevance.DEC-02: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit rule on caseworker home entry and consent during a child protective investigation.
relevance.FAIL-02: It is the principal Fourth Circuit authority a Virginia family must distinguish when claiming an unconstitutional entry or search preceded a removal.

cases.case_name: Hodge v. Jones
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit reversed, holding that a state agency's continued retention of child abuse investigation records after a report is ruled out or unsubstantiated violates neither substantive nor procedural due process, because retention serves legitimate child welfare interests and confidentiality provisions prevent any cognizable stigma.
cases.quote: The record before us presents no substantive due process violation of a familial privacy liberty interest by virtue of the retention of the Hodge investigation report.

relevance.INP-02: It addresses the consequences for a family of a third-party report that was investigated and then ruled out.
relevance.INP-06: It holds that an anonymous or ultimately unsubstantiated report may nonetheless leave a permanent agency record without constitutional violation.
relevance.DEC-01: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit authority that a screened-out or unsubstantiated file may lawfully be retained by the agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: It relies on statutory confidentiality regimes to hold that retained records inflict no actionable stigma, which frames how disclosure failures should be assessed.
relevance.PMC-05: It marks the constitutional floor on record retention and access, against which state transparency rules operate.
relevance.PMC-06: It is essential background for any analysis of Virginia CPS data retention, since the Constitution imposes no purge requirement for unfounded reports.

cases.case_name: Martin v. Saint Mary's Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed qualified immunity for two social workers involved in removing children without a court order, holding over a dissent that the plaintiff had not established a violation of a clearly established constitutional right on this record.
cases.quote: We have held that social workers may assert qualified immunity in appropriate circumstances.

relevance.DEC-04: It illustrates how thin the record must be before a court will excuse a removal effected without prior judicial authorization.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the Fourth Circuit's principal modern statement that social workers performing discretionary removal functions may claim qualified immunity, and the dissent states the competing substantive due process rule.
relevance.FAIL-04: It sets the qualified immunity hurdle that governs damages claims against caseworkers for decisions made about children in their charge.

cases.case_name: Doe ex rel. Johnson v. South Carolina Department of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit recognized that a child involuntarily removed from her home has a substantive due process right not to be placed in a known, dangerous foster care environment in deliberate indifference to her safety, but held the caseworker entitled to qualified immunity because that right was not clearly established at the time.
cases.quote: had a corresponding duty to refrain from placing her in a known, dangerous environment in deliberate indifference to her right to personal safety and security

relevance.ACT-03: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit statement of the constitutional duty owed to a child once the state places her in foster care.
relevance.ACT-06: The child's psychiatric hospitalization and treatment history were central to what the agency knew about the danger of the placement.
relevance.OUT-04: For youth who remain in state care, it supplies the substantive due process duty of reasonable safety that continues throughout the placement.
relevance.OUT-06: It is the governing circuit authority on agency liability for serious harm suffered by a child while under state supervision.
relevance.FAIL-03: It is the principal vehicle in this circuit for testing whether federal child welfare obligations translate into individually enforceable rights.
relevance.FAIL-04: It defines deliberate indifference — notice of a danger plus a choice to ignore it — as the standard for harm to a child in agency custody.
relevance.PMC-01: Systemic placement failures of the kind described here are exactly what federal safety and permanency monitoring is designed to detect.

cases.case_name: Weller v. Department of Social Services for the City of Baltimore
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit held that a father stated a procedural due process claim where the state deprived him of custody of his child for four months with no judicial action ratifying the deprivation, and that the domestic relations exception did not bar his § 1983 damages claim.
cases.quote: an utter lack of judicial action ratifying the deprivation of custody for four months is clearly not the prompt due process that the Constitution requires

relevance.INP-12: It fixes the outer bound of lawful protective custody: emergency action must be followed promptly by judicial ratification.
relevance.DEC-04: It is the circuit precedent Jordan v. Jackson relies on for the rule that emergency removal is permissible only if prompt post-deprivation process follows.
relevance.FAIL-02: This is the foundational Fourth Circuit case establishing that a prolonged custody deprivation without judicial review is actionable under § 1983.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the Due Process Clause imposes no affirmative obligation on a State to protect a child from violence by a private actor, even where the agency knew of the danger, absent a custodial relationship that limits the child's freedom to act on his own behalf.
cases.quote: But nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors.

relevance.OUT-04: The custody-based exception the Court describes is the doctrinal source of any continuing state duty toward youth who remain in care.
relevance.OUT-06: This is the governing federal rule limiting constitutional liability when a child known to the agency is killed or seriously injured by a parent.
relevance.FAIL-04: It is the controlling authority a family must overcome to hold a Virginia agency constitutionally liable for a child's death after agency involvement.
relevance.PMC-04: Because constitutional damages liability is foreclosed in most non-custodial cases, fatality review and legislative reform are the principal accountability mechanisms.

cases.case_name: Suter v. Artist M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court held that the 'reasonable efforts' clause of the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act, 42 U.S.C. § 671(a)(15), creates no federal right enforceable by private individuals under § 1983 or directly under the Act.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.INP-09: Because private enforcement is unavailable, federal review and audit are the operative checks on a state's reasonable-efforts performance.
relevance.FAIL-03: This is the controlling authority that federal child welfare funding conditions are enforced through the Secretary and federal review, not private suit.
relevance.PMC-01: It is the reason CFSR monitoring rather than litigation is the principal remedy for a state's failure to meet federal performance standards.
relevance.PMC-02: Federal audit and funding penalties are the enforcement route the Court left intact after foreclosing private actions.
relevance.PMC-03: Citizen review panels exist in part because the federal statute itself confers no privately enforceable rights.
relevance.PMC-06: Any accountability analysis of Virginia's federal compliance must account for the absence of a private right of action under Title IV-E.

cases.case_name: Haaland v. Brackeen
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court rejected all challenges to the Indian Child Welfare Act, upholding Congress's authority to enact it and its application in state court proceedings on the merits, and dismissing the equal protection and remaining placement-preference challenges for lack of standing.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners’ challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling authority that ICWA validly binds Virginia state courts whenever the child is an Indian child, including its placement preferences and evidentiary standards.
relevance.FAIL-03: It confirms that ICWA's mandates apply to state agencies and courts as federal law, so non-compliance is a federal compliance failure.
relevance.FAIL-05: The Court disposed of the race-based equal protection attack on ICWA's placement preferences for lack of standing, leaving those preferences operative.
relevance.PMC-01: ICWA compliance is a federally monitored dimension of state child welfare performance, and this decision leaves that framework fully in force.

cases.case_name: Rocka v. Roanoke County Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed an order granting a welfare board permanent custody with the right to place for adoption, holding that in a contest between a parent and a non-parent the rule of comparative best interests does not apply and the board must prove parental unfitness by clear and convincing evidence, and directing an interlocutory award of custody to the mother so she could demonstrate her present fitness.
cases.quote: We believe that the evidence of parental unfitness in this record is less than clear and convincing and, thus, insufficient to divest a parent of custody of its child.

relevance.INP-05: The mother herself asked the Board to take her children and place them in foster care until she could find work and a home, and the Court held that request could not be converted into permanent severance without proof of unfitness.
relevance.ACT-03: It governs the Virginia foster care placement that begins as a parent's voluntary request for temporary help and later becomes a board petition for permanent custody with the right to place for adoption.
relevance.OUT-01: The Court ordered an interlocutory award of custody to the mother for at least six months so she could demonstrate her capacity, the clearest early Virginia statement that reunification is the default when the agency's proof falls short.

cases.case_name: Berrien v. Greene County Department of Public Welfare
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed an order terminating a mother's parental rights and entered final judgment restoring custody to her, holding that even though credible evidence supported the trial court's best-interests finding, the Department bore and failed to carry the burden of proving parental unfitness before rights could be permanently terminated.
cases.quote: the burden was on the Department to prove Berrien's unfitness before the trial court could take the ultimate, drastic, and irrevocable step of permanently terminating her parental rights

relevance.ACT-02: The juvenile court had awarded the mother custody on a court-supervised 'probationary period of indeterminate length' to verify she was providing a suitable home, and the Court measured the Department's case against what that supervision actually produced.
relevance.OUT-01: Rather than remand, the Court ordered custody of the child restored to her natural mother, the strongest Virginia authority that reunification follows when the agency fails to prove unfitness.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court expressly declined to remand for another evidentiary hearing and brought the pending litigation to a conclusion, the appellate equivalent of closing an unproven case.

cases.case_name: Shank v. Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the denial of a natural mother's petitions for custody and to intervene in her children's adoption, holding that an unappealed commitment order providing for permanent separation severs all parental rights, is immune from collateral attack except on jurisdictional grounds, and leaves the parent a legal stranger to the child.
cases.quote: the second remedy authorizes a severance of all parental rights, including the right to place for adoption and the right to consent to adoption

relevance.INP-12: The Department took the infants into protective custody on complaints of child abuse and placed them in foster homes, and the opinion traces how that emergency action ripened into a permanent-separation order.
relevance.ACT-03: It distinguishes a commitment that only suspends custody, from which a parent may later reacquire the child by showing changed circumstances, from a commitment for permanent separation, and that distinction governs the legal effect of every Virginia foster care order.
relevance.ACT-04: The Department placed the boys in the home of their paternal uncle and aunt, who then petitioned to adopt, and the Court held the mother had no cognizable defense or claim entitling her to intervene in that kinship adoption.

cases.case_name: Malpass v. Morgan
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia reversed a decree allowing a stepfather to adopt over the natural father's objection and dismissed the adoption petition, holding that although the child's welfare is of paramount concern, the condition applicable in parent versus non-parent custody contests applies equally in adoption cases.
cases.quote: The condition is that the rights of parents may not be lightly severed but are to be respected if at all consonant with the best interests of the child.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the foundational Virginia rule for adoption over a natural parent's withheld consent and the doctrinal predecessor of both Doe v. Doe and Copeland v. Todd.
relevance.OUT-03: A non-parent seeking to convert de facto care into permanent legal status must satisfy the condition that parental rights not be lightly severed, which is the ceiling on any Virginia guardianship or kinship permanency claim.
relevance.OUT-05: The Court did not remand but dismissed the adoption petition outright once the showing against the natural parent failed.

cases.case_name: Kaywood v. Halifax County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that the three statutory prima facie triggers are not the only means of proving that the conditions causing the abuse cannot be corrected, and that whether correction is possible 'within a reasonable time' is judged from the context and attendant circumstances.
cases.quote: The phrase, “within a reasonable time” is not definable by any prescribed rule. Its meaning depends upon the context and the attendant circumstances; not upon mere opinion or expectation.

relevance.ACT-01: The father argued the Department never offered or provided him any rehabilitative services, and the Court held that the absence of that statutory prima facie trigger does not by itself defeat a subsection (B) case.
relevance.ACT-06: The infant was found in a pitiful condition and in need of immediate medical care, and the father's failure to seek any medical treatment for him was part of the proof that conditions could not be corrected.
relevance.OUT-06: The child had been seriously abused and injured to the point that his life was in danger, and the opinion shows how that degree of injury shapes the prospective judgment a Virginia court must make.

cases.case_name: Toms v. Hanover Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination under Code § 16.1-283(B), holding that rehabilitative services are a relevant concern but not an absolute prerequisite to a subsection (B) termination and that due process imposes no constitutional duty to provide them, while distinguishing subsection (C), which turns on the parent's failure to remedy problems during a period in which services were offered.
cases.quote: subsection C requires the court to determine whether the parent has been unwilling or unable to remedy the problems during the period in which he has been offered rehabilitation services

relevance.ACT-01: It is the Virginia authority separating the two statutory tracks: the offer of services is the measure under subsection (C), but is a relevant factor rather than a condition precedent under subsection (B).
relevance.ACT-02: Counsel litigating the adequacy of a court-approved service record must first identify which subsection is in play, because only subsection (C) measures the parent's response to the services actually offered.

cases.case_name: Fields v. Dinwiddie County Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination entered under both Code § 16.1-283(C)(2) and § 16.1-283(E)(i), holding that an (E)(i) termination requires clear and convincing proof that termination is in the child's best interests together with a finding that the parent's rights to a sibling were previously terminated, which substitutes for proof that the parent failed to remedy the conditions leading to foster care.
cases.quote: In addition, the trial court must find the parent's rights to a sibling of the child previously had been terminated.

relevance.ACT-02: It shows that where a parent's rights to a sibling have already been terminated, the sufficiency of the current court-approved service plan and the parent's response to it drop out of the Department's case entirely.

cases.case_name: Jenkins v. Winchester Department of Social Services
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed both an abuse-and-neglect finding as to a newborn removed days after birth and the termination of the mother's rights to an older child, holding that the statutory definitions require no proof of harm already suffered because 'substantial risk' speaks prospectively and Code § 16.1-251(A)(1) contemplates removal before the child enters the dangerous environment.
cases.quote: We agree with the Department that the statutory definitions of an abused or neglected child do not require proof of actual harm or impairment having been experienced by the child.

relevance.INP-07: The Department filed its petition the day after the child's birth at the Winchester Medical Center based on its prior experience with the mother, the paradigm hospital-based opening of a Virginia case on a newborn.
relevance.INP-12: The newborn was taken under an emergency removal order entered two days after birth, and the Court held Code § 16.1-251(A)(1) authorizes exactly that pre-harm protective custody.
relevance.DEC-04: This is the Virginia authority that a child may be removed before being placed into an environment where severe or irreversible injury would be likely, based on the parent's history rather than injury already inflicted.
relevance.DEC-05: The Department opened the case by petition alleging abuse and neglect under Code § 16.1-228(1) and (5) and requesting custody, and the Court upheld that route and rejected a challenge premised on defects in the later foster care plan.

cases.case_name: Logan v. Fairfax County Department of Human Development
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed termination and the award of custody to the Department rather than the maternal grandmother, holding that a parent retains standing to contest the placement that accompanies termination and that under Code § 16.1-283(A) the Department must produce sufficient evidence about available relatives for the court to compare relative placement against other options, a duty satisfied on this record.
cases.quote: the Department has a duty to produce sufficient evidence so that the court may properly determine whether there are relatives willing and suitable to take custody of the child

relevance.ACT-04: This is the controlling Virginia statement that the burden of identifying and evaluating relatives rests on the Department, not on the parent, before a court places a child outside the family.
relevance.ACT-06: The case arose from the mother's repeated failure to obtain necessary and available medical and physical therapy services for a child with cerebral palsy, and from the court's order compelling her to take him to his hospital appointments.

cases.case_name: James v. Jane
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia held that the immunity of state employees is qualified rather than absolute and that a simple negligence claim is tested by examining the function the employee performed, the extent of the state's interest and involvement in that function, and the degree of state control, concluding that attending physicians at a state hospital were not immune.
cases.quote: Under such circumstances we examine the function this employee was performing and the extent of the state's interest and involvement in that function.

relevance.FAIL-04: This is the four-factor test itself, which any damages claim against a Virginia child welfare worker for harm to a child in care must run before Messina's extension to local-government employees can even be applied.
relevance.PMC-02: The distinction it draws between the state's absolute immunity and an employee's qualified, function-dependent immunity is what determines whether agency conduct can be tested in damages litigation or only through audit and oversight.

cases.case_name: Watson v. Shepard
cases.holding: The Supreme Court of Virginia affirmed the denial of a mother's petition to regain custody, holding that because a prior juvenile court order entered after her voluntary relinquishment, an investigation and a hearing had altered her custody rights she bore the burden of showing changed circumstances, but reversed the interlocutory adoption decree because the prospective adoptive parents were separating.
cases.quote: the burden was not upon the Shepards, as the mother argues, to show parental unfitness

relevance.INP-05: The mother's own voluntary written relinquishment of custody, acted on after a thorough investigation and a hearing, is what shifted the burden against her when she later asked for her child back.
relevance.ACT-04: The child had been placed with her paternal aunt and uncle, and the Court held those kinship custodians bore no burden of proving the mother unfit, while still refusing to let their adoption proceed with their own marriage unsettled.

cases.case_name: Vosburg v. Department Of Social Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fourth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Virginia social workers, holding that they are absolutely immune from § 1983 liability arising from their decision to file a removal petition because that function is prosecutorial, while expressly declining to extend that immunity to their conduct in investigating whether a petition should be filed.
cases.quote: We emphasize, however, that our grant of absolute immunity applies only to those activities of social workers that could be deemed prosecutorial.

relevance.DEC-02: The Court expressly refused to immunize the investigation that precedes a removal petition, which is why the investigative stage remains the litigable part of a Virginia CPS case.
relevance.DEC-05: This is the controlling Fourth Circuit holding that under Virginia law the filing of a removal petition is the start of judicial proceedings and an advocate's act carrying absolute immunity.
relevance.FAIL-02: A Virginia wrongful-removal claim cannot be built on the decision to petition, so it must attack the investigation or the seizure itself.
relevance.FAIL-04: It fixes the immunity line governing damages claims against Virginia caseworkers, and the Court expressly left open whether that immunity reaches their conduct in caring for a child after removal.

cases.case_name: Stadter v. Siperko
cases.holding: The Court of Appeals of Virginia affirmed the denial of visitation to a former partner who was not the child's parent, declining to adopt a de facto or psychological parent doctrine in Virginia and holding that a non-parent must first prove actual harm from denial of visitation before any best-interests analysis may be applied over a fit parent's objection.
cases.quote: The evidence supporting non-parent visitation must therefore be sufficient to overcome the constitutional concerns inherent in the Troxel presumption

relevance.ACT-04: It establishes that a relative or other caregiver in Virginia acquires no parental constitutional status from caregiving alone, which limits what a kinship placement can later be converted into.
relevance.OUT-03: Relied on by name in Mast v. A.A., it is the Court of Appeals' statement that a person who is not an actual parent has no constitutional claim to the child and must clear the actual-harm threshold.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Supreme Court reversed, holding that 'domicile' in ICWA § 1911(a) is defined by uniform federal law, that children born off the reservation take the reservation domicile of their parents, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction so the state adoption decree had to be vacated under 25 U.S.C. § 1914.
cases.quote: We therefore think it beyond dispute that Congress intended a uniform federal law of domicile for the ICWA.

relevance.INP-11: This is the controlling federal authority on when ICWA strips a state court of jurisdiction altogether, and it holds that parents cannot defeat exclusive tribal jurisdiction by arranging an off-reservation birth and adoption.
relevance.FAIL-03: An adoption entered by a state court that lacked ICWA jurisdiction must be vacated under 25 U.S.C. § 1914, the sharpest illustration that ICWA non-compliance is a federal-law failure with a statutory remedy.

notes: All 37 cases in this brief were retrieved from CourtListener on 2026-09-21 and the full opinion text of each was read. Every quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved majority opinion text (quote marks, apostrophes, dashes and whitespace normalized). No quote is drawn from a syllabus, headnote, dissent, concurrence, party brief, or the court's characterization of a prior case.

No unpublished memorandum decisions were used. Every entry is a published opinion of the Supreme Court of Virginia, the Court of Appeals of Virginia (which publishes only a fraction of its family-law docket), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit, or the U.S. Supreme Court.

Three Virginia opinions in CourtListener carry no reporter citation in their cluster record and are given in slip form: Bonanno v. Quinn (Record No. 200963), Mast v. A.A. (Record No. 240707), and Norfolk Department of Human Services v. Goldberg (Record No. 1382-23-1). All three are published opinions; Goldberg and Mast will appear in Va. App. and Va. respectively, but the reporter volume and page were not available from the cluster, so they are not asserted here.

OUT-04 (extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18) has NO on-point Virginia case law. Targeted searches of both va and vactapp for juvenile court jurisdiction past age eighteen, Fostering Futures, and transitional services returned nothing responsive. The node is therefore mapped to the federal standard: Doe ex rel. Johnson v. South Carolina DSS (continuing substantive due process duty of reasonable safety toward a child the state has placed), DeShaney (custody as the source of any affirmative duty), and Suter v. Artist M. (no private enforcement of Title IV-E obligations). Virginia's extended foster care program rests on Va. Code §§ 63.2-905.1 and 16.1-283.3 and on 22VAC40-201, which have not been construed in a published opinion located in this session.

INP-11 (ICWA / tribal jurisdiction) has no Virginia state-court decision applying the Indian Child Welfare Act that could be located in CourtListener. Virginia has no state ICWA statute. The node rests on Haaland v. Brackeen for the Act's validity and binding force on state courts, plus Mast v. A.A. for the Supreme Court of Virginia's most recent handling of competing external (federal/foreign) claims to a child placed and adopted in Virginia. Practitioners must work directly from 25 U.S.C. §§ 1911-1915 and 25 C.F.R. Part 23 for active efforts, qualified expert witness testimony, placement preferences and transfer to tribal court. Note also that Santosky records that ICWA sets a beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard for termination of an Indian child's parental rights, higher than Virginia's clear-and-convincing standard.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the VA node files (e.g. 'In Re: Hargrove', 'Doe v. Green' with synthetic citations such as 'Virginia Supreme Court Case 240316 (2025)' and Justia URLs) are keyword-matched noise. None was retrievable as an on-point child welfare authority and none is carried forward. Every case in this brief replaces them.

Virginia's CPS administrative track and its juvenile court track are legally distinct and should not be conflated. A 'founded' disposition under Va. Code § 63.2-1526 is reviewed under the Administrative Process Act for substantial evidence (Turner v. Jackson; Commissioner v. Fulton), applies a preponderance standard at the agency (22VAC40-705-10), and by itself changes no custody or parental right (Jackson v. W.; Turner v. Jackson). Termination of residual parental rights under Va. Code § 16.1-283 requires clear and convincing evidence in a juvenile or circuit court (Knox; Toombs; Christopher Farrell). Cases from one track do not supply the standard for the other.

Two structural traps for counsel: (1) the burden of proof. On appeal from the juvenile and domestic relations district court the circuit court tries the termination petition de novo and the Department carries the clear-and-convincing burden; a prior custody order does not shift it (Walker v. Department of Public Welfare). (2) Prima facie triggers. Richardson holds that proof of certain statutory facts is prima facie evidence of the § 16.1-283(B)(2) conditions, but Harris holds that undisputed evidence the agency offered a parent no services overcomes that prima facie case and puts the Department to full proof — the single most useful defensive holding in the Virginia termination line.

The § 1983 authority for Virginia is Fourth Circuit law. Jordan v. Jackson is a Virginia case and upholds the seventy-two hour statutory scheme facially, so a Virginia wrongful-removal claim generally cannot be built on delay alone; it must attack the absence of imminent danger at the moment of removal (see the Martin dissent for the competing substantive due process formulation) or a deprivation extended without any judicial ratification (Weller). Wildauer forecloses most Fourth Amendment challenges to a consented caseworker home visit. Hodge forecloses challenges to retention of unfounded-report records.

State-law tort claims against Virginia local social services employees run into Messina v. Burden: a supervisory or discretionary employee of an immune governmental entity acting within the scope of employment is immune from simple negligence, so a complaint must plead gross negligence or intentional misconduct.

Aggravated circumstances matter enormously in Virginia. Under Va. Code § 16.1-283(E), as applied in Yafi, a felony conviction for child abuse causing serious bodily injury to the child or a sibling removes the reasonable-and-appropriate-efforts element from the Department's case entirely. Counsel should check subsection (E) before litigating reasonable efforts under (B) or (C).

Kinship placement in Virginia is governed by four express statutory findings that must be stated in the order (Lynchburg Division of Social Services v. Cook, construing Va. Code §§ 16.1-278.2(A1), 16.1-281(C1), 16.1-282(D1), 16.1-282.1(A1)). Tackett adds that a relative caregiver, even a former guardian, has standing only as to the permanency goal and her own custody petition, not to contest termination of the parent's rights. These two cases together control almost every contested Virginia kinship dispute.

Records and transparency: Norfolk DHS v. Goldberg (2024) is the current leading Virginia authority on Code § 63.2-1514(D) and holds that the bad-faith disclosure exception reaches allegations laundered through an innocent mandatory reporter. Department of Corrections v. Surovell supplies the general VFOIA construction rule (liberal construction toward disclosure, narrow construction of exemptions, agency bears the burden by a preponderance). Neither has been applied to a child-fatality review record in a published opinion located here.

Several nodes in the PMC family (PMC-01 through PMC-06) and FAIL-03 concern federal oversight architecture rather than adjudicated rights. No court, state or federal, has adjudicated Virginia's CFSR performance, its Citizen Review Panels under CAPTA § 5106a(c), or its fatality review commission in a published opinion located in this session. Those nodes are mapped to the closest governing authority — Suter v. Artist M. (no private enforcement), Surovell (records access), Jackson v. W. (judicial review of the Department's own guidelines and policy manual), Hodge v. Jones (record retention), DeShaney and Doe v. SCDSS (limits of constitutional liability) — and should be read as supplying the legal frame, not as holdings about Virginia's oversight bodies.
Coverage check: all 42 nodes carry between 2 and 6 cases; 37 distinct cases are used; no node is padded with an authority that was not read in full.
